entry.title: Alvin Says!
entry.content:
Why should Simon have all the fun? In Alvin Says!, all three chipmunks join in, giving you simple commands that are easy to mess up. Keep them fed with nuts to increase your score — but be aware, one wrong move and it's game over!

How to Play

Alvin Says! is a game all about reaction time.

The objective is to keep the chipmunks fed. Successfully completing their commands will replenish their supply of nuts. However, If you take too long or press the wrong button, they'll run out of nuts, and you'll lose!

What makes things tricky is that the chipmunks don't all communicate in the same way:

  • Alvin likes to show rather than tell, so you should press the button which matches the colour of his command.

  • Simon likes to keep things practical. He'll just tell you which colour to press.

  • Theodore may be small, but he can be tricky. You must press either of the buttons which match neither what he shows nor what he says.

If the prompt doesn't come from any of the chipmunks, it's because they're out gathering. Just wait out the time and they'll replenish the nuts themselves.

It sounds like a lot at first, but you'll soon get the hang of it. Good luck!

Downloads

If you're using Android, Windows or Linux, you can also download the game to play offline on your device. Click on the appropriate button to download the latest release of Alvin Says! for your operating system.

entry.title: Class or Culture: Explaining Support for Right-Wing Populism
entry.summary: An essay analysing factors contributing to increasing support for right-wing populist parties across Western democracies
entry.content:
Author's Note This essay was awarded 1st Place in Politics by St Hugh's College, Oxford in the 2025 Kavita Singh Essay Competition.

Introduction

The rise of the populist right is one of the defining political developments of the twenty-first century. From Trump to Le Pen, Orbán to Wilders, parties once dismissed as fringe have entered the political mainstream — winning elections, reframing public discourse, and polarising electorates and commentators alike. Their ascent has prompted intense academic debate, especially over the question of why they have gained such wide and durable support. One prominent answer points to economics: that decades of stagnating wages, industrial decline, and welfare retrenchment have created a class of citizens who feel materially excluded, and who turn to populist movements as a reaction against the failures of neoliberal globalisation.

This essay argues that while economic conditions help set the stage for populist mobilisation, support for the populist right is ultimately driven moreso by deeper cultural and social anxieties. Right-wing populists politicise economic grievances through narratives of national decline, cultural betrayal, and demographic change — placing immigration, law and order, and social cohesion at the centre of their appeal.

Download PDF

The Core Argument

In the full analysis, I evaluate the "Cultural Backlash" thesis against the "Losers of Modernisation" perspective, specifically looking at:

  • Structural Conditions for Populist Mobilisation

  • The Limitations of Class-Based Explanations

  • The Role of Populist Economics

  • Immigration and Cultural Drivers

Conclusion

The populist right draws its strength from the convergence of several factors: institutional openness, charismatic leadership, economic grievance, and a widespread loss of faith in mainstream political representation. Yet if we are to prioritise among these, the conclusion is unambiguous: economic determinants are not the principal drivers of support for the populist right. What unites their supporters is not a shared vision of political economy, but a shared sense of cultural dispossession — a belief that national identity, social order, and familiar norms and values are under threat.

In the end, we cannot understand support for the populist right without examining the economic landscape in which it operates. But nor can we explain it if we stop there. The grievances that fuel populist politics are not simply demands for more money or better jobs, but for recognition, belonging, and symbolic restoration. Indeed, to understand the populist right, we must look not just at what people have lost, but at what they feel has been taken from them — and at who they believe is to blame.
